title: Accenture Splits Salary Hikes for 780,000 Employees Between Base Pay and Lump Sum
excerpt: The global IT services giant is dividing approved raises equally between a permanent base pay increase and a one-time cash payout, a shift that affects roughly 350,000 employees in India.
body:
• Accenture will split approved salary increases 50/50 between a permanent base pay hike and a one-time lump-sum cash payout in June.
  • The change affects more than 780,000 employees globally, including roughly 350,000 in India.
  • Promotion-linked raises will continue to be delivered entirely through base pay, and the lump-sum payment will not replace December bonuses.
  • The move comes after Accenture gave limited “stay-at-level” increases last year, and is designed to extend raises to a larger share of its workforce.

A New Compensation Playbook

Accenture has overhauled how it distributes salary increases, splitting approved raises equally between a permanent base pay increase and a one-time lump-sum cash payout — a structural shift that touches its entire global workforce of more than 780,000 people, according to an internal memo reviewed by PTI and The Times of India.

Under the new model, if a talent lead approves a 3% increase for an employee, 1.5% will be added to base salary and the remaining 1.5% will be paid as a one-time cash amount during the June compensation cycle.

“We are both significantly increasing the number of people who receive stay-at-level increases and delivering the increase in two parts: half as a base pay increase and half as a one-time lump sum paid in June.”

— Accenture, Internal Memo

Why the Split?

The restructuring comes after a lean year. In the previous compensation cycle, Accenture offered limited raises to employees who stayed at the same level — a move widely felt across India’s IT workforce. This year, the company says it is “significantly increasing” the number of employees receiving raises while changing the delivery mechanism to manage its overall payroll burden.

Accenture framed the lump-sum component as a benefit employees have asked for: immediate cash. By splitting the approved increase, the company can reward more people without a proportional rise in its recurring salary obligations — a balancing act familiar to any large employer navigating macroeconomic uncertainty.

What Stays the Same

Promotion-linked pay increases remain untouched and will continue to flow entirely into base salary. The one-time lump-sum payment will not replace annual performance bonuses awarded during the December cycle. Both the base pay increase and the lump-sum component will count towards FY26 bonus calculations, and the lump sum will be subject to standard deductions for employees enrolled in the Voluntary Equity Investment Program (VEIP) or the Employee Share Purchase Plan (ESPP).

Compensation decisions will still be made by talent and group leads based on skills, performance, business impact and employee behaviours — the same criteria as before.

Mixed Reactions Among Employees

The change has drawn divided responses. Some employees welcomed the prospect of immediate cash, while others questioned whether the arrangement is temporary or will become a permanent feature of future cycles. A key concern is the long-term impact: since only half the approved increase becomes part of recurring salary, compounding base-pay growth slows over time.

Tax implications have also surfaced as a worry, though sources familiar with the decision told The Times of India that the compensation change is unrelated to India’s labour code provisions.

The Bigger Picture for India’s IT Workforce

Accenture employs roughly 350,000 people in India — nearly half its global headcount — making it one of the country’s largest private-sector employers. Any shift in its compensation strategy sends a signal across the broader IT services industry, where peers like TCS, Infosys and Wipro are also navigating the balance between rewarding talent and managing costs amid a still-uncertain demand environment driven by the West Asia crisis and global economic headwinds.

For Indian tech workers abroad and those considering moves between companies or geographies, Accenture’s approach could become a template. Whether other firms follow suit will depend on how employees respond and whether the model proves sustainable over multiple cycles.
